# 2 Maccabees Chapter 4 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** The Simon mentioned above, who had informed about the money and about his fatherland, slandered Onias as if he had been the one who incited Heliodorus and had been the instigator of the trouble.

**2** He dared to call this benefactor of the city, protector of his compatriots, and zealot for the laws an enemy of the state.

**3** But when his enmity went so far that murders were being committed by some of Simon's approved men,

**4** Onias, recognizing the danger of the contention and that Apollonius as the son of Menestheus and governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia was inflaming Simon's wickedness,

**5** betook himself to the king, not as an accuser of his compatriots but looking to the general and particular welfare of all the multitude.

**6** For he saw that without the king's attention it would be impossible to obtain peace in affairs nor for Simon to cease from his folly.

**7** But when Seleucus departed from life and Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, took over the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias obtained the high priesthood by corrupt means,

**8** promising the king three hundred and sixty talents of silver and from some other revenue eighty talents.

**9** In addition to this he promised to pay one hundred and fifty more if permission were given him through the king's authority to set him up a gymnasium and a body of youth for it, and to enroll the Antiochenes in Jerusalem.

**10** When the king consented and he came to power, he at once shifted his compatriots over to the Greek way of life.

**11** And setting aside the royal concessions to the Jews, secured through John the father of Eupolemus, who went on the mission to establish friendship and alliance with the Romans, he annulled the lawful ways of living and introduced practices contrary to the law.

**12** For with alacrity he founded a gymnasium right under the citadel, and he induced the noblest of the young men to wear the Greek hat.

**13** There was such an extreme of Hellenization and increase in the adoption of foreign ways because of the surpassing wickedness of Jason, who was ungodly and no true high priest,

**14** that the priests were no longer intent upon their service at the altar. Despising the sanctuary and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful proceedings in the wrestling arena after the call to the discus,

**15** disdaining what their fathers had honored and thinking the Greek forms of prestige to be the finest thing.

**16** For this reason a heavy disaster overtook them, and the very men whose ways of living they emulated and desired to imitate in everything were their enemies and punished them.

**17** For it is no light thing to act impiously against the divine laws — the time that follows will make this clear.

**18** When the quinquennial games were being held at Tyre and the king was present,

**19** the vile Jason sent as spectators three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice to Hercules. Even the bearers thought it improper to use the money for the sacrifice, and considered it better to devote it to some other purpose.

**20** So the money intended by the sender for the sacrifice to Hercules was, by the decision of the bearers, applied to the construction of triremes.

**21** When Apollonius the son of Menestheus was sent to Egypt for the coronation of King Philometor, and Antiochus learned that Philometor had become hostile to his government, he went to Joppa, and from there to Jerusalem.

**22** He was welcomed magnificently by Jason and the city and ushered in with a blaze of torches and with shouts, and from there he marched with his forces into Phoenicia.

**23** After a period of three years Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the Simon mentioned above, to carry the money to the king and to get decisions on certain necessary matters.

**24** But he, being introduced to the king, when he appeared to him as a man of dignified bearing and was advanced in wisdom, secured the high priesthood for himself, outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver.

**25** So he came back with the royal mandate but bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood. He had the temper of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.

**26** Jason, who had supplanted his own brother, was now supplanted by another man and driven as a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites.

**27** And Menelaus held the office, but he paid nothing of what he had promised to the king,

**28** though Sostratus the governor of the citadel kept demanding it — for to him belonged the collection of the revenues — and because of this both were summoned before the king.

**29** Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as deputy in the high priesthood, while Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cyprian troops.

**30** While such was the state of affairs, it happened that the people of Tarsus and of Mallus made an uprising because their cities had been given as a present to Antiochis the king's concubine.

**31** So the king went hurriedly to settle the trouble, leaving Andronicus, a man of high rank, to act as his deputy.

**32** But Menelaus, thinking he had obtained a good opportunity, presented to Andronicus some of the gold vessels of the temple which had been taken from it; he had already sold some to Tyre and to the neighboring cities.

**33** When Onias became aware of this, he reproved him, having withdrawn to a sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch.

**34** Therefore Menelaus, taking Andronicus aside, urged him to kill Onias. He went to Onias, and using treachery and swearing oaths, he gave him his right hand in pledge and persuaded him, notwithstanding his suspicion, to come out from the sanctuary; and at once he dispatched him, with no regard for justice.

**35** For this reason not only the Jews but many also of other nations were indignant and displeased at the unjust murder of the man.

**36** When the king returned from the region of Cilicia, the Jews in the city, with the Greeks who shared their feelings, appealed to him; they were grieved that Onias had been killed without cause.

**37** So Antiochus, grieved at heart and moved to pity, wept because of the sobriety and great propriety of the deceased.

**38** And inflamed with anger, immediately he stripped Andronicus of his purple and tore off his garments, and leading him throughout the whole city to the very place where he had committed the outrage against Onias, there he put the bloodthirsty fellow to death. The LORD rewarded him with the punishment he deserved.

**39** When many sacrilegious acts had been committed in the city by Lysimachus with the connivance of Menelaus, and when the report of them had spread abroad, the populace gathered against Lysimachus, since many of the gold vessels had already been dispersed.

**40** When the crowds were rising in revolt and becoming filled with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and launched an unjust attack, with one Auranus as leader, a man advanced in years and no less advanced in folly.

**41** When they realized the attack of Lysimachus, some picked up stones, others blocks of wood, others took handfuls of the ashes that lay there, and threw them all in a promiscuous confusion at Lysimachus and his men,

**42** with the result that they wounded many of them, and killed some, and put all the rest to flight, and the temple plunderer himself they killed near the treasury.

**43** Charges were brought against Menelaus about this affair.

**44** When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the council of elders presented the case before him.

**45** But Menelaus, already as good as convicted, promised a substantial sum of money to Ptolemy son of Dorymenes to persuade the king.

**46** Therefore Ptolemy, taking the king aside into a colonnade as if for refreshment, induced him to change his mind.

**47** Menelaus, the cause of all the evil, he acquitted of the charges against him, while those unfortunate men, who would have been freed even if they had argued their case before Scythians, he condemned to death.

**48** Thus those who had spoken for the city and the villages and the holy vessels quickly suffered unjust punishment.

**49** And for this reason even the Tyrians, detesting the crime, provided magnificently for their burial.

**50** But Menelaus remained in office owing to the covetousness of those in power, growing in wickedness, having become the chief plotter against his fellow citizens.
